The president hasn’t done much to help, and his poll numbers have plunged, even on the economy and immigration, his usual strengths. Republicans, fearing hostility, have largely opted to forgo town halls this summer, skipping what tends to be an effective way to reach constituents. A few of those who have held gatherings in their districts have faced anger and tough questions about Iran, including why the U.S. launched the war in the first place.

Republicans have been urging the White House to wrap up the conflict and reduce its drag on the nation’s economy—and their reelection chances. But a solution has proved elusive. Trump’s goals for the conflict were never well enunciated and have shifted many times. Gone are lofty promises about regime change or preventing Iran from having a nuclear program. Instead, the president has privately told his political allies that once the Strait of Hormuz is reopened, he is inclined to simply declare victory and move on, one outside adviser and a senior administration official told us on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. But even that has proved vexing: Iran has continued to menace ships traveling through the strait and has insisted upon charging a fee or toll. Other countries in the region have declared that unacceptable—the strait was, after all, open and free before the war—though Trump has waffled on whether or not he could live with it. The president said yesterday that the last of the Iranian mines had been removed from the channel, but an official from a country in the region stressed to us that even if that were to remain true, Iran could still terrorize ships with small boats, handheld rocket launchers, and drones.

Republicans have signaled to the White House their approval of its new economic pressure campaign, which was announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this week. The White House’s political shop hopes the plan creates a quiet stranglehold—Bessent deemed it “economic asphyxiation”—that could make steady progress in resolving the conflict while having the added bonus of keeping it out of the headlines. (Trump’s bellicose threats toward Iran have unfailingly driven news cycles and hurt Republicans.) Some in the administration believe that emerging divides in Tehran’s leadership could prompt talks. And if the new sanctions did bring Iran to the table before November, then maybe a renewed stab at diplomacy could juice the markets—and provide an 11th-hour boost for Republicans.

Trump has been bored of the war for a while. Aides have been pushing him to focus on the economy to help Republican candidates, but he has continued to downplay the nation’s affordability challenges, much to his aides’ chagrin. And while Trump remains furious at Iran’s unwillingness to bend, aides have persuaded him to give the new plan a chance. In some ways, it’s not an original idea: Trump has relied on an economic “maximum pressure” campaign since his first term to try to force Iran to abandon its nuclear program. But the intelligence community was mistaken in its belief that Iran would buckle quickly under the financial strain. The regime seems willing to endure significant hardship, and its own citizens’ struggles, to maintain its grip on power. And the new approach carries its own political risks. If Iran proves resilient again, the pressure campaign may have to stretch beyond the midterms, leaving prices high in the interim.

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told us in a statement that the United States has already “destroyed Iran’s military capabilities” and is now “strangling what’s left of its abysmal economy” by severing its remaining financial lifelines. “They will stand alone, broke, and isolated,” Wales wrote. “The President has been clear: he will always advance America’s interests and never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

The U.S. military has not struck Iran in weeks. This month’s relative reprieve follows a long pattern of using force to try to extract concessions from Iran and failing. After a 13-day strike campaign in July, the U.S. military privately assessed that extending the campaign would lead to diminishing returns—and worsen the nation’s extraordinary munitions shortage.

Earlier this month, Steve Feinberg, the No. 2 leader at the Pentagon, sent a memo demanding that the defense industry rapidly expand its production. Over the course of the war, the U.S. has used many of its Tomahawks, drones, and air-defense munitions. A July 27 assessment by the Center for Strategic and International Studies concluded that the war has significantly depleted U.S. air-defense stocks—particularly of Patriot and THAAD interceptors—and that replenishing those munitions to prewar levels would take years. Last week, Raytheon announced it had been awarded a $22.9 billion contract that would “dramatically accelerate the production of Tomahawk cruise missiles.” Still, the administration insists its stockpile is robust.

There have been other costs to the American military: Eighteen service members have been killed, and bases in the region have been damaged. The USS Abraham Lincoln’s 5,000 sailors and Marines spent more than 270 consecutive days at sea without a port visit; the carrier’s extended deployment was marked by reports of food and supply shortages, plumbing problems, and declining morale. Only in recent days did it leave the region, bound for Asia, though the U.S. is keeping two aircraft-carrier strike groups nearby—the USS George Washington and the USS George H. W. Bush.

Iran has also largely stopped its strikes toward U.S. bases across the region. Last week, the United Arab Emirates said that Iran had launched two ballistic missiles that splashed down in the Persian Gulf, one within the Emirates’ territorial waters—the last known instance of Iranian aggression (though Tehran denied involvement). On Monday, an oil tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Omani shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz, damaging its engine room and disabling the vessel. The crew was unharmed, and no one has yet claimed responsibility.

Trump has never been one to show much discipline, and could lose patience with the waiting game. But Iran also gets a say in determining what happens between now and November. More punitive American sanctions are likely to provoke a response from Iran, particularly because its leaders want the U.S. to feel the costs of the war. Iran is also watching the midterm elections closely; some officials fear that Trump could become more aggressive in the weeks after ballots are cast. That could prompt Iran to escalate first—and once more put the war back into voters’ minds.

entries.title: Why Was This Looney Tunes Movie Almost Shelved for Good?
entries.summary: The director of Coyote vs. Acme wants to make sense of the film’s near death.
entries.content:
The director of Coyote vs. Acme wants to make sense of the film’s near death.

Perhaps the starkest sign that Coyote vs. Acme isn’t your typical children’s movie is that it’s based on a New Yorker article. Yes, it features many Looney Tunes characters that multiple generations know and love, interacting alongside real-life actors in a style similar to prior big-screen efforts, such as Space Jam or Looney Tunes: Back in Action. But the director Dave Green’s film—which opens August 28, after a protracted saga that almost saw it kept from audiences forever—draws from a slyly funny “Shouts & Murmurs” story from 1990. Written by the humorist Ian Frazier, “Coyote v. Acme” has a wry and self-aware premise: What would happen if Wile E. Coyote, the Looney Tune on a constantly unsuccessful hunt for the ever-chipper Road Runner, filed a lawsuit against the (fictional) Acme Corporation for selling him faulty products?

“I thought the baseline idea for the movie was just, like, the funniest thing in the world,” Green told me in a recent interview, reminiscing about when he first signed on to direct the film, back in 2019. He wasn’t the first person in the film industry to be charmed by Frazier’s story. Despite the erudite tone, the simple notion of Wile E. Coyote pursuing legal action was amusing enough to Hollywood producers that various attempts were made to develop it for the screen, dating back to an effort by the producer Scott Rudin in the late 1990s.

Warner Bros., which owns Looney Tunes, jump-started the latest version of the project in 2018, and Green completed it in 2022. Coyote vs. Acme was initially scheduled to debut the following summer, but it was taken off the schedule early into production; a new release date was never announced. In the fall of 2023, Warner Bros. told the director that the movie would be shelved entirely. The studio reportedly made the call for a tax write-off—the latest in a series of such decisions, as it dealt with debt issues after the pandemic.

Three years later, Coyote vs. Acme is finally entering theaters. After years of limbo, it ended up in the hands of Ketchup Entertainment, an independent distributor that has now become its unlikely savior. The company cut a $50 million deal with Warner Bros. for it last March. “I continued to not believe it, up until now, when I still can’t believe it,” Green said. “It’s a completely surreal reality to check into. But it seems to be happening—I think it’s happening,” he added with a laugh.

His trepidation is understandable: The path the film took to cinemas reflects Hollywood’s continued post-pandemic instability, even as theatergoing has picked back up. Coyote vs. Acme had reportedly tested well with audiences and featured some of Warner Bros.’ most well-known creations, yet the cancellation suggests the company still expected to lose too much money on the project.

The wildest part of the production, Green admitted, was how easy it was at first. When asked by Warner Bros. to pitch ideas for an adaptation of Frazier’s article, the director proposed something along the lines of a true-crime documentary crossed with a legal drama. To his surprise, the studio didn’t immediately turn him down. “It almost felt like everything was a ‘yes,’ and there were no boundaries. So then I got really excited,” Green said. “They were looking for a take and they were looking for something that would help them narrow in. And, as different as my tonal comparisons were, I think they responded to the fact that there was a take in it.”

Green’s notion was to take the tropes of underdog courtroom movies—he cited The Insider, Erin Brockovich, and A Few Good Men as inspirations—and place cartoon characters within them. The humans they interact with (played by Will Forte, Lana Condor, and John Cena, among others) would treat Wile E. Coyote’s lawsuit with humdrum seriousness. “That’s the kind of behavior that really comes from Looney Tunes historically,” Green said—winking references to grown-up media that its young audience might not understand. “It’s Bugs Bunny in Casablanca or Elmer Fudd at the opera, poking at high art.” That device has become a hallmark of the franchise, with self-aware comedy making up the bulk of its spin-off Tiny Toon Adventures and of Looney Tunes’ spiritual successor, Animaniacs.

The devious extra twist of Coyote vs. Acme, however, comes from watching the Looney Tunes themselves navigate human society, with its mundane rules and morals. The story is set in Albuquerque, and the live-action sequences were shot almost entirely on location, lending the kind of jarring verisimilitude Green was hoping for—the animated elements pop against the dusty backdrop. Wile E. Coyote is still capable of speaking only through hand gestures and written signs, but he’s hoping to get a personal-injury lawyer named Kevin Avery (Forte) to help him sue Acme; the manufacturing company is presented as a corporate juggernaut that sells products to both humans and cartoons, while gleefully cutting corners in the name of profit.

The result is explosively zany. It’s also surprisingly sensitive—a quality often lacking from the anarchic Looney Tunes. In bite-size animated form, Wile E. Coyote has a monomaniacal obsession with destroying the Road Runner that’s designed to be a recurring, villainous gag; here, it’s a sad compulsion, a habit he cannot kick. The turn works because it doesn’t feel dark, but rather sweetly relatable. “What if you treated Wile E. like a person and his pain as real?” Green asked. “Then that kind of led to the path of, like, what if it’s about cartoon characters being treated unfairly? That kind of split the whole thing open in a fun way.”

Green shot the movie in spring 2022, an experience he describes as entirely pleasant. “There was actually a lot of support from even the very highest-up voices at the studio, and they were really positive in reacting to my initial cut,” he recalled. Yet that summer, Warner Bros. made the surprising decision to shelve Batgirl, a $90 million HBO Max production. “That was really scary to us,” Green said. “But we never thought we were in the same danger.” Batgirl seemed plagued by various other corporate maneuvers: a shift away from movies produced exclusively for streaming, and a general impending reset of the DC Comics cinematic universe. (Analysts also believed that Warner Bros. intended to take a write-down on Batgirl, to help alleviate its multibillion-dollar debt.) Still, the decision alarmed many filmmakers, who now had to worry that studios might choose to just delete their work instead of bothering to release it.

Coyote vs. Acme was initially slated to debut July 21, 2023, before Warner Bros. decided to put Barbie in that summer slot. After that, Green remembered, his cast and crew waited for a rescheduled date, which never came. Finally, in November, the studio told him that Coyote vs. Acme would not be released at all. A public outcry from both fans and members of the industry quickly pressured Warner Bros. to shop the movie to other distributors, including Amazon, Apple, and Netflix. The studio’s price tag, however, was reportedly too high for these potential buyers, and Warner Bros. eventually rejected all competing bids to hand it over—an apparent death sentence for Coyote vs. Acme.

Green recalled a fellow director comforting him during this period by saying, “You got away with it. You robbed the bank. You made a courtroom drama for kids starring Looney Tunes characters. In so many ways, this movie should not exist.” Still, as Green told it, the thinking behind pulling Coyote vs. Acme was never fully clear to him. Although it is more complex than a typical kids’ film, the good test-viewing scores and positive critical reception suggest there’s an audience for it. Ketchup Entertainment can’t afford the large marketing budget that a more established studio could have; it is likely looking to recoup costs through international sales and at-home rentals. That Warner Bros. abandoned all of this goodwill and earnings potential, to Green, was somewhat baffling.

But he feels lucky to have finished the film—which he called an “impossibility” for its blend of classic Looney Tunes absurdity and legal-thriller influences—in the first place. Now it has finally escaped containment; Green, it seems, has successfully rewritten his movie’s real-life ending.

entries.title: The Jason Arday Truthers
entries.summary: The concerted effort to airbrush the late fabulist’s life
entries.content:
In death, Jason Arday has become two people. To many readers of legacy newspapers, the late Cambridge University academic is a proven fabulist. The life story on which he built his career, of being nonverbal until 11 because of autism, and then learning to read at 18 and becoming a professor, has “no precedent in medical literature,” as The New York Times delicately put it. Among many other extraordinary claims, his tale of being menaced by a knife-wielding man at Cambridge could not be corroborated, and neither could the story that his family had received a pig’s head as an act of racist intimidation. “To be honest with you, I thought you’d just believe me,” he told a Guardian reporter who challenged him.

That is one reality. However, another one dominates left-wing new media, activist nonprofits, and visual social networks such as Instagram and TikTok. There, the prevailing narrative is that Arday did nothing seriously wrong and Britain’s right-wing media hounded an exceptional Black scholar to his death on August 14 for no reason except racism. Well-wishers have raised more than $300,000 for his family, and made his upcoming memoir a best seller in Britain. At a rally in central London held in his memory, attendees carried placards reading Rest in Power Professor Jason Arday, even though he had resigned the title days before his death. They wanted to make clear their belief that he was unfairly deprived of his academic status.

For some of Arday’s supporters, acknowledging that any of the media scrutiny was justified has become tantamount to siding with his “killers.” He is instead a martyr—the victim of a “lynching”—and the inconvenient fact of his fabulism must be tidied away from the virtual shrine. This is an emotional position rather than a rational one, and its very indefensibility makes it a greater demonstration of tribal loyalty. Insisting that the academic was completely innocent, in the face of all the evidence, sends a strong social signal that you hate the right-wing media and care about racism.

The central question in this dispute is whether the treatment of Arday—the subject of more than 200 articles in print this year, according to CNN, and hundreds more online—was proportionate. The smaller his alleged offenses, the more easily one can argue that the media hounded him to death. And so Arday has been recast as a small-time plagiarist; academics have lined up to argue that, You know, even that isn’t a very big deal. The “meaning of plagiarism does not cover mere overlap of sentences,” the academic Jason Stanley asserted in a blog post that also bizarrely noted that he hadn’t paid much attention to the story because he had been on vacation in Europe. Stanley’s blithe dismissal will be news to students who are told the exact opposite early in their courses. Or to Ross Barkan, who was dropped from New York magazine after getting caught recycling other writers’ words.

Another popular declaration is that Arday “was cleared of plagiarism” by Liverpool John Moores University, where he received his doctorate. This is technically true. When concerns were raised about his dissertation, Cambridge University declined to investigate, saying it was a problem for Liverpool John Moores, which had already stated that it stood by his work. Just before Arday’s death, however, Cambridge reversed its position, pledging to investigate, as did other institutions that had employed Arday. (Arday then resigned from Cambridge, adding that the move should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me.”) Stressing that he was “cleared” misses the point; the exact allegation is that universities’ lack of interest in scrutinizing Arday represented a failure of institutional checks. Now anyone can run Arday’s thesis through plagiarism-detection software themselves and make up their own mind. When Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, a writer who otherwise found the media coverage racist, did so, he concluded that “Arday was definitely guilty.”

Keeping a narrow focus on the doctoral thesis is helpful to the pro-Arday side. He also faced a far more serious charge of academic fraud—that he lifted interviewees’ quotations from a 2016 paper in BMJ Open and inserted them into the mouths of people he had supposedly spoken with in his own research, implying outright fabrication of interviews that never occurred. After Cambridge was made aware of this accusation in 2023 by other academics, the journal Social Sciences took an Arday paper offline and then uploaded it again with the offending quotations excised and other direct quotes edited. (Another paper of his in a different journal was also subsequently corrected.) Arday essentially admitted to the misattribution by agreeing to the amendments, although he had earlier told the researcher who raised the issue that questioning him was “bullying and harassment.”

The postmortem airbrushing of Arday’s story also ignores how that story twisted and turned while he was alive. When The Guardian confronted him with the implausibility of some of his tall tales, Arday responded by editing them in real time: Yes, he had once claimed to have run 600 miles in six days, an exceptional feat for an endurance athlete, but what he actually meant was that he took daylong rest breaks in between. Yes, he had claimed to have raised more than £5 million for charity, but actually this was with the help of “many fundraising collectives” whose participants he could not name because they had signed nondisclosure agreements.

The Arday partisans have seized on the thinnest of straws. Defending his philanthropic record, the Byline Times, a British website that bills itself as offering “what the papers don’t say,” implied that the relevant charities’ huge fundraising capacity made his claims credible. “A Byline Times analysis of the publicly identifiable charities Arday was associated with for two decades found that they had a combined gross income of approximately £1.4 billion to £1.5 billion,” it reported, “putting his £5 million collective fundraising claim at well under 1% of their overall income.” That sensation you can feel is your brain melting out through your ears and trickling down your neck. The same analysis would uphold my claim to have, say, just donated six fighter jets to the U.S. government, because they cost a minuscule fraction of the nearly $1 trillion defense budget. Why would you doubt me?

One of the biggest promoters of the revisionist narrative is the Good Law Project, a nonprofit chiefly known in Britain for its patchy record of challenging legal decisions, and for the unforgettable viral incident in which its founder, Jolyon Maugham, voluntarily confessed to having beaten a fox to death with a baseball bat while wearing his wife’s kimono. The Good Law Project intervened on Arday’s behalf early in the news cycle, describing the initial coverage as a “malicious” witch hunt based on “fake accusations of plagiarism.” It mustered an open letter in his defense.

What followed was a classic Streisand effect: The newspapers defended themselves by seeking further corroboration of Arday’s fabulism. As the allegations mounted, various signatories disappeared from the letter, indicating that they found the evidence concerning. By August 8, Maugham was distancing himself, saying that his decision to “carry—a deliberately neutral verb—an open letter in support of Dr Arday” relied on Cambridge’s judgment. He stated that he had not personally evaluated Arday’s broader trustworthiness. “It is expedient for me to say, but it is also true for me to say, that: I only last night returned from ‘holiday,’” he wrote.

After Arday’s death, though, Maugham also offered a new statement, in which he had in fact been closely involved with the letter, and furthermore had intervened in the hope of dissuading the left-wing Guardian from publishing its own damning exposé of Arday. The stated rationale was that the academic was vulnerable, that the right was already attacking him, and that Arday believed (without offering any evidence) that the Guardian reporter Lanre Bakare had a beef with him.

Some people seem to think this was reasonable—that the subjects of unflattering articles should get to veto their publication. Journalism cannot work this way. Maugham’s failed attempt to spike a story on Arday’s behalf became yet more fodder for the narrative of the evil, racist press versus Jason the Martyr. Never mind that Bakare is himself of African descent, or that, as a note hastily appended to Maugham’s statement acknowledged, Arday had initially approached Bakare with his story about the pig’s head and the marauding knifeman.

The academic had wanted his story in the public domain—but only if the journalist endorsed it. Bakare’s real offense was finding no evidence for Arday’s outlandish claims, and saying so.

Why dwell on this depressing, convoluted saga? Many people will be thinking: The poor guy quit, and now he is dead. First, because Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, is still advertised for sale on Amazon UK with absolutely no mention of the controversy surrounding its wild claims. (Arday’s family wanted to continue with publication.) “That oft-used word ‘inspirational’ feels wholly inadequate to describe his incredible story of grit and resilience,” an endorsement sourced from the industry publication The Bookseller declares.

The word incredible is the correct one: My colleague Dan Engber reported how several of the most eye-catching claims in the book’s proposal were swapped for different, but equally dramatic, claims in the finished text. (Arday’s publisher did not respond to his questions about the changes.) As Engber wrote:

The proposal also lays out many of the same events as the memoir but with slightly different dates and details: The boys who beat him up were not his age but four years older; his suicide attempt happened before, not during, the pandemic. And whereas the book describes Arday as having survived two brain tumors, the proposal says he had a bout of testicular cancer. No reference to that illness appears in the memoir.

Nor does the book describe the time that Arday, then a teenager, was struck by a car and spent several months in a coma.

A second reason that the story still resonates is that Arday’s death—the version of it in which he is a complete innocent, hounded by feral, racist journalists—is now being used for political purposes in Britain. The Good Law Project and its allies have demanded the resignation of Cambridge’s vice-chancellor for failing to support Arday; the defenestration of various journalists who covered the story or edited the newspapers in which it appeared; and a public inquiry into Arday’s death, with the desired outcome being tighter restrictions on what the press can publish. Groups affiliated with Amnesty UK have even endorsed “Arday’s Law,” whereby the number of news articles on any person would be capped. This proposal is nonsensical. Do activists really believe that, if The New York Times has used up the entire press’s monthly Trump-scandal quota, everyone else should fall silent?

The Arday case is endlessly debatable because it contains so many double-edged elements. Yes, the academic—one of relatively few Black professors in Britain—was subject to extra scrutiny because of his race. Equally, though, Arday absolutely traded on his identity and his life story. “In his keynotes, Arday focuses on how his identity as a Black autistic man has shaped his experiences in the academic world,” the blurb on his (since-deleted) profile at the Simon & Schuster Speakers Bureau reads.

Undeniably, many of Arday’s detractors treated him not as a fallible human but as a stand-in for the debate over diversity, equity, and inclusion. The academic whose Substack post kicked off the coverage, Nathan Cofnas, is a “race realist” who reveled in the fact that he had taken down someone he saw as the beneficiary of a corrupt, anti-white system. When I asked Cofnas why he had decided to immolate his career by arguing that Black people are academically inferior to white people, he told me that “wokism is the ideology of taking the equality thesis seriously” and that “the only way to defeat the destructive ideology of wokism is to show that it is based on a false empirical premise.”

A few days before we spoke over email, Cofnas was suspended by Ghent University, in Belgium, where he is a postdoctoral scholar, because of the negative publicity he had generated. This news caused widespread rejoicing on the left: A lot of onlookers who were until that moment very opposed to people losing academic jobs amid media storms suddenly decided that this phenomenon was, in fact, good. (An open letter is currently in circulation defending Cofnas.)

Without question, the media coverage of Arday was harsh and high-volume. But much of that volume came from competing outlets breaking fresh news, as more and more of Arday’s extraordinary claims crumbled under scrutiny. Some commentators have argued that coverage ought to have stopped after his resignation. I feel differently; the reporting should (and I think would) have stopped if he admitted to the fabulism. But Arday died still maintaining that he had never lied, and his memoir is on sale, untroubled by corrections to anecdotes that now seem enormously implausible.

Unfortunately, unlike Arday’s fabrications, anti-Black racism in Britain is only too real. But you can believe in that without believing in Jason Arday.

entries.title: The Truth About Dolly Parton’s Style
entries.summary: It wasn’t about showbiz. It was about sovereignty.
entries.content:
Dolly Parton was just 5-foot-nothing tall. She needed platform heels to make her feel that she could fill a performance space. Her husband, Carl Dean, once told her that from the audience, her platinum wigs made her tiny figure look like a Q-tip. But no amount of mocking could make her surrender the hair, heels, and rhinestones, which were her own brand of feminism under wraps. “Believe it or not, I had to fight for that look!” she wrote in her 2023 memoir, Behind the Seams.

The look wasn’t about showbiz. It was about sovereignty. And it must have been more than passingly rewarding for Parton to know that her audience finally understood this about her before she died, at the age of 80—to know that she was fully appreciated for the wallop of woman she was. She had so much guts, smarts, and self-ownership beneath the taffetized country-music artifice that sold more than 100 million records.

There was no hint of glamour in the Tennessee hill country where Parton grew up, just unadorned, worn-out women like her mother, who’d married at 15 and had a dozen children by the age of 35. Parton’s first dresses were made of flour and feed sacks. Too poor to buy real makeup, Parton would use pokeberry juice to redden her lips and the burned end of a matchstick to do her brows. When her sharecropper father caught her, he’d whip her and try to wash it off. “Back then, any woman who wore makeup in the mountains was considered trashy,” she wrote. “But I didn’t care.” She’d plead to her dad that it was “her natural color.” He’d snap, “‘Natural color,’ my ass! You get in there and get that off of you.”

After she began to make some money from singing bits on Knoxville’s popular Cas Walker Farm and Home Hour, she went to the local drugstore to buy herself some Maybelline. Store-bought makeup and clothing that fit her form gave her courage. She wrote, “I remember feeling powerful enough to go up against Daddy or Grandpa to say, ‘Now, that’s not that tight. It ain’t cut that low. It ain’t that much.’ And they’d say, ‘Yes, it is!’ But I’d be willing to get my ass whupped for it.”

She wore anything gaudy that she could lay her hands on. An unusually candid photo of Parton, taken early in her career, shows her eyes painted with large half-moons of blue, reflective eye shadow. Her earrings are as big as saucers. Her hair is bound with a purple headband, and her head is tilted at a cocky angle as she stares straight and unsmiling at the camera. It is a portrait of not a girl but a challenger, a young woman of utter defiance. You weren’t going to catch that Dolly being bullied by classmates for the “coat of many colors” that her mama had sewn out of rags. You could bet she wasn’t going to stay under the dirt-caked thumb of her father, in that cabin that had no plumbing or electricity, for much longer, either. Her mother understood. She’d surreptitiously sew a little sass and lift into those homemade clothes: “Now, don’t tell your daddy I put some push-ups in that dress.”

The day after Parton graduated high school, she packed everything she had in four grocery bags from the Piggly Wiggly and caught the bus to Nashville. “My matching luggage,” she called those paper sacks. Her rise to stardom in Nashville probably came with more sexual harassment than anyone will ever know. She spent seven years accompanying Porter Wagoner on his hit TV show and then had the sense to wrest herself out of his domineering hands. “I couldn’t just stay there forever being somebody’s girl singer,” she wrote about her break with Wagoner. She added, “I never was one to be told what to do for too long because I never could do what anybody else told me to do if it went against who I am.” In a 2023 interview with The Guardian to promote her book, she said: “I always knew how to put a man in his place without making him feel bad. If sometimes that don’t work, I’m also strong as a boy—I know how to push you off and get the hell away from you.”

She was strong enough to withstand Wagoner when he sued her for leaving his show and she had to settle with him for $1 million, strong enough to reject Elvis Presley when he demanded half of her publishing rights to record her song “I Will Always Love You,” and strong enough to resist all of the advice from agents and record moguls who wanted her to tone down her look. She turned the tables on people who made fun of her—“You’d be surprised how much it costs to look this cheap,” she said—and earned the nickname “Iron Butterfly.” She amassed a collection of more than 200 wigs. When people asked her how long it took to do her hair, she quipped: “I don’t know. I’m never there.”

With that in mind, listen anew to “Jolene.” It’s got all of Parton’s fabulous contradiction in it, the arch-femininity paired with command. What a mistake to take the song’s traditional “please don’t take my man” superficial pleading as weakness. Trumping the lyrics is Parton’s soaring voice and that galloping triplet rhythm. It might be her most deceptively powerful song.

Parton never called herself a feminist. She rejected the label for much the same reason that she was steadfastly apolitical, at least in public. She couldn’t stand to be told who she was or what to say. She said in her Guardian interview that once you pick a political side, “you’re not allowed to think nothing else. Well, how crippling is that?” When Barbara Walters asked her in 1977 why she continued to court derision with her garish getups, Parton said: “I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable. That’s the easiest thing in the world to do.”

The simple truth of Parton’s style is that it made a diminutive, rags-poor girl from the backwoods feel bold enough to explore her gorgeous flute of a throat and sing in public. As her career progressed, she found her own voice in endeavors including acting and philanthropy. Being “under the lights, you want to feel important,” she wrote. The stage “makes me want to try to live up to my shiny clothes. It’s like, okay, you got on this outfit. You’re going to have to rise to the occasion.” Rise, she did.

entries.title: The German Far Right Is Poised for a Breakthrough
entries.summary: The AfD could do something next month that would mark a first in the country’s postwar history.
entries.content:
The AfD could do something next month that would mark a first in the country’s postwar history.

Imagine that it’s October 2026, and one of Germany’s 16 federal states has come under the control of a far-right government for the first time since the Nazi era. With an absolute majority in the state Parliament and one of its own installed as state premier, the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, quickly begins implementing its agenda. The interior minister announces an emergency remigration program: abolishing asylum, revoking the residence permit of any foreigner convicted of a crime, pledging to review all naturalization decisions made during this century, and incarcerating those designated for deportation. The government stops classifying Ukrainians as war refugees and ends their social benefits. European Union flags disappear from public buildings. The mainstream press is shunned in favor of influencers aligned with the party’s ideology. The government authorizes vigilante groups to act as an auxiliary police force in regions with high crime rates.

This hasn’t happened, but it’s not merely hypothetical either. The AfD is projected to win an election next month in Saxony-Anhalt, a central German state of some 2 million people. An anti-racism NGO in Berlin, the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, created this scenario based on the far-right party’s own election manifesto and the statements of its representatives. For decades, right-wing politics have carried particular weight in Germany, where atonement for the Holocaust includes mandatory education about the rise of National Socialism. The far right was long relegated to the fringes, its most ardent members easily identified as skinheads decked out in leather. But the AfD, founded in 2013 as a mild euroskeptic party led mostly by conservative economists opposed to eurozone bailouts, is now Germany’s most important right-wing force since the Nazis.

At the national level, the AfD is the most popular party, supported by more than a quarter of voters in recent polls. It leads both of the traditional broad-based parties, the center-right Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats. Its base of support is in the formerly Communist east—generally poorer, older, and angrier than the rest of Germany. And that’s where it’s poised for a breakthrough later this summer. In past state elections, other parties have contorted themselves to keep the far-right faction out of governing coalitions, maintaining a so-called firewall even when the AfD has won the most votes. That may not be possible in Saxony-Anhalt, where ahead of a September 6 vote, the AfD is polling at more than 40 percent. If smaller parties fail to reach the required 5 percent threshold to enter Parliament, this kind of showing by the AfD could be enough for it to win an outright majority, meaning that it wouldn’t need cooperation from other parties to govern. Suddenly, Saxony-Anhalt would become a testing ground for AfD policies.

If the AfD doesn’t reach that threshold, the spotlight would turn to the Christian Democratic Union, the party of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The Christian Democrats would face a dilemma: whether to breach the firewall and work with the AfD or join hands with the far-left party Die Linke in a last-ditch effort to keep the far right from taking power. In fact, the Christian Democrats have a policy, formalized in 2018 and known as an incompatibility resolution, against working with either party. Andreas Rödder, a historian who previously headed the center-right party’s fundamental-values commission, told me that the decision didn’t generate much controversy within the party at the time because the matter was mostly symbolic; the center-right party, then dominated by Chancellor Angela Merkel, had other choices for governing partners. At that time, German politics remained fairly stable, relatively speaking, as anti-establishment forces shook up other Western democracies. For many in Germany, this was a point of pride, a sign that the country had learned from its history, that it knew where political fanaticism led.

Less than a decade later, Germany no longer appears immune to extremism, and the stable politics that once attested to its moral redemption are “on the brink of being fundamentally shattered,” Rödder said. The country’s domestic intelligence agency has classified Saxony-Anhalt’s branch of the AfD as a right-wing extremist group. Some voters support the party because of that hard-right agenda. Others are drawn to it for contrarian reasons: to register their dissent against elite gatekeepers, whether in the security service, the judiciary, or the media. In this way, their vote is a version of the declaration once made by the Russian literary critic Vissarion Belinsky: “Negation is my god.”

“Every organ of elite opinion tells people they can’t vote for the AfD,” a German diplomat told me. “And many people respond by saying, ‘Hell yes, we can.’”

Why does an election in a relatively small German state matter? Because what happens in Germany matters. That’s been the nature of the German problem for almost two centuries—what to do with this country, larger and more prosperous than its neighbors, that has caused so much torment for Europe and for the world. The problem arose with the Franco-Prussian War and the unification of Germany in 1871. It returned in monstrous form during both world wars. And it recurred with German reunification in 1990.

The German question is back as the country breaks with postwar taboos. Germany is rearming, spending billions to turn its army into the strongest in Europe. Its steadfast support for Israel has been shaken by the extremism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. And in Saxony-Anhalt as well as other German regions, even if not yet nationally, the far right appears on the cusp of claiming power.

Germany’s situation isn’t unique; what’s striking in a country where historians have debated whether a Sonderweg, or “special path,” produced destructive nationalism is how much it mirrors what’s happening elsewhere in Europe. Marine Le Pen, the far-right French firebrand, is leading in polls ahead of a presidential election next year. Nigel Farage’s Reform UK remains in a strong position in Britain. Giorgia Meloni already leads a far-right government in Italy, representing a party that traces its roots to the country’s postwar neofascist movement. Saxony-Anhalt is following these same trends. But the circumstances command greater attention. As Henry Morgenthau Jr., President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s treasury secretary, titled his postwar book on the defeated Axis power, Germany Is Our Problem.

Saxony-Anhalt is sometimes called the heartland of German history. It’s the birthplace of the Protestant Reformation, where Martin Luther nailed his 95 theses to the church door in Wittenberg. Cities such as the capital, Magdeburg, were important centers of the Holy Roman Empire. In the 20th century, modernism flourished in the region, which has Germany’s highest concentration of Bauhaus architecture. It’s long been a hub of the chemical and coal-mining industries. During the Cold War, the territory fell on the eastern side of the Iron Curtain, and the state still faces structural problems left over from post-reunification deindustrialization and out-migration, including higher rates of poverty and unemployment than the national average. The psychic effect also lingers. Until 1990, there was no genuine democracy; freedom and civil rights were curtailed. “In some quarters,” Detlef Gürth, a member of the ruling Christian Democrats in Saxony-Anhalt’s state Parliament, told me, there is still a “pronounced desire for a ‘strongman,’ a messiah who dictates the course of action and takes care of everything.”

Two recent events crystallize the state’s misfortune and the feeling among many residents that things aren’t working. In December 2024, a Saudi-born doctor drove a rented SUV through a crowded Christmas market in Magdeburg, killing six people and injuring hundreds more. Authorities said the perpetrator was an anti-Islam activist sympathetic to far-right groups, but terrorist violence of any kind, the facts notwithstanding, played into the far right’s hands. The following year, the California-based Intel Corporation canceled plans for a €30 billion chip factory in Magdeburg, which would have been the biggest-ever foreign direct investment in Germany. The episodes were unrelated; the company said it had simply grown too fast, although a government minister also found an explanation in “Donald Trump’s ‘America First’ philosophy.” Together, however, they contributed to a gathering feeling of precarity and bad luck.

The AfD promises to shake up the system. Its 35-year-old front man, Ulrich Siegmund, is a perpetually smiling social-media sensation. He is a salesman by trade, the founder of a fragrance company called Berlin-Duftet, whose name means literally “Berlin smells good.” Der Spiegel, the prestigious German news magazine, recently branded him “the most dangerous man in Germany,” which turned out to be great publicity; at campaign events, he autographed copies of the magazine cover.

As Siegmund racks up likes on social media, he leaves the most incendiary topics to others in the party. When some members of the state AfD branch traveled to the United States last year to attend a gala of the Trump-aligned New York Young Republican Club, Siegmund stayed home. The party’s ideological engine in Saxony-Anhalt is said to be Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a member of the state Parliament who has likened Islam to a fungus, condemned the “sacralization of the Holocaust,” and suggested that Jewish institutions are using Muslim immigration to achieve the “abolition of our people.” He has called AIDS patients the “price we pay for a decadent social model” and argued that the Bauhaus movement “raped the human need for comfort.” On foreign policy, Tillschneider sides with Russia in its assault on Ukraine, praising President Vladimir Putin as “a real man with a sound set of values” and insisting that Moscow is “defending itself.”

When I asked Tillschneider to explain his party’s success in the region, he said it didn’t stem from one particular issue or another but amounted to a rejection of the mainstream’s whole approach to policy making. He argued that the “established parties have formed a consensus against the interests of the citizens” and refuse to entertain ideas that go against their orthodoxy. The AfD is testing the limits of what’s acceptable in German political culture, especially on immigration. The party’s election manifesto declares ominously, “Our streets and squares are no longer safe.” And it promises a “deportation and remigration offensive.” The term remigration, once a fringe concept linked to ethnic cleansing, is now a focus of far-right immigration discourse, and has flexible meanings. Tillschneider defined it as “the maximum possible deportation within the framework of the constitutional order.” In addition to a “180-degree turn” in migration policy, the party is also vowing to revamp education and art, instill pride in German identity, and end the country’s “guilt complex.” The AfD also objects to the established parties’ anti-Russia policies and seeks to expand Russian-language instruction in schools and revive student exchanges with Russia.

The Christian Democrats, who currently govern Saxony-Anhalt in a coalition with the Social Democrats and the liberal Free Democrats, have struggled to respond. The state premier, Sven Schulze, took umbrage at the far right for “constantly belittling Saxony-Anhalt and acting as if everything here is doomed to failure.” AfD representatives can sense the desperation. Tillschneider said the firewall had become a “tomb wall” that the Christian Democratic Union has built for itself. He envisioned only two possibilities after the September election: either an AfD government or an “all-party government against us.” On this there seems to be some agreement. Gürth, the Christian Democratic lawmaker, said his party can’t justify cooperation with the AfD, which “operates like the Nazi Party” in its methods: “It exaggerates real or perceived problems, taps into public discontent, and paints a dystopian picture of Germany teetering on the brink of collapse. All other parties are blamed, and only the AfD can save Germany.”

In the scenario outlined by the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, an AfD-led government soon turns the state into a platform for international self-promotion, hosting conferences and opening offices in Washington and Moscow. Vice President Vance, who met with an AfD leader on the sidelines of the Munich Security Conference last year, visits the state and offers to support American companies that choose to invest in Saxony-Anhalt. In the next federal election, in 2029, the AfD wins. The party may soon get the chance to give this scenario a shot.

entries.title: Trump Plans to Buy Midterm Ads About His Own Record
entries.summary: The president has come up with a simple plan to win the election: more Trump.
entries.content:
The president has come up with a simple plan to win the election: more Trump.

President Trump gathered his top political advisers in the Oval Office early this month to solve a problem of riches: how to spend his super PAC’s $400 million political war chest with fewer than 100 days to go before the midterm elections.

Republican strategists are concerned about Trump’s low approval ratings and voter anxiety about the economy. One person familiar with the Oval Office strategy meeting put it this way: “When the issues that you typically campaign on don’t move voters—or voters are pissed off at you about those issues—the question becomes: What do you campaign on?” Some GOP strategists favor focusing entirely on specific races in an effort to convince voters of the merits of individual candidates and local issues.

But Trump himself has rejected that approach. House and Senate Democrats, the president noted during the meeting, will make their fall campaigns a referendum on him. His advisers told him that the poor polling reflects the fact that the voting public still does not know about many of his accomplishments—the dozens of new stock-market highs, a decline in fentanyl deaths, the “sealed” southern border, the increase in domestic-manufacturing production.

The solution Trump settled on, according to three people familiar with the meeting, was to lean into the Democratic strategy of focusing on himself. The president ordered a series of television advertisements about his own record that will serve as a backdrop to the hundreds of individual House and Senate contests. Trump wanted what one person described to us as “environmental lift” ads—commercials that would focus on nationalizing the midterms broadly around his victories—and he suggested that the ad makers mine his own on-camera statements as building blocks. “Go look at the clips,” the president told his team, according to this person. “I cite accomplishments all the time.”

That decision has resulted in a Trump midterm-election ad blitz that is set to be rolled out soon from MAGA Inc., the main repository of Trump’s political fundraising, according to people familiar with the discussions, all of whom insisted on anonymity to describe internal conversations. Most of MAGA Inc.’s spending is still expected to go to targeted House and Senate races, for which the group has been establishing teams to review polling, voter modeling, and message testing. “We are going to unload the guns on both chambers real soon,” one of the people said. But another person told us that because Trump will inevitably be part of voters’ considerations, highlighting his achievements makes sense. “I think everybody does understand that the president and his agenda are on the ballot to some degree,” another person told us.

A spokesperson for MAGA Inc. told us that the group does not comment on internal deliberations or plans. Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told us that Trump is committed to maintaining the Republican majorities in Congress. “President Trump is cleaning up Joe Biden’s mess,” she said in a statement. “There is a great story to tell because the United States of America has never been stronger than under his leadership.”

Trump’s decision to focus a portion of his spending on himself echoes President Biden’s decision in the fall of 2023 to launch a series of ads trumpeting his own legislative record, as he sought to increase his approval rating in advance of his reelection bid. But Trump is not on the ballot this fall, which presents new risks. A new strategy of touting Trump’s achievements could well backfire by aiding Democratic efforts to make each race about national issues at a time when Trump’s approval rating is at record lows. Yet given the midterm headwinds, Republicans may have little choice but to present their most effective communicator to voters.

The political climate—an economic election in which voters don’t feel that their life has gotten better, despite some positive indicators—is in many ways similar to what Democrats faced in 2010 and 2022, when the electorate blamed their party for the economic pain of the 2008 financial crisis and the coronavirus pandemic, respectively. But in other ways, the situation Trump faces is different. Polls show that voters aren’t just anxious about inflation; they are frustrated with Trump’s war of choice with Iran and concerned about government corruption. Before Trump’s first midterm election as president, in 2018, the Pew Research Center found that 51 percent of the country believed that the economy was doing well, including 13 percent who described the economy as excellent. By July of this year, only 22 percent felt that the economy was doing well, and only 3 percent described it as excellent. Trump’s economic approval rating hovered at about 50 percent in 2018 public polls. Most polls this year show that his standing has fallen into the 30s.

Republican political consultants have voiced concerns both publicly and privately in recent weeks about the triumphant tone of some of Trump’s economic messaging. Democrats see a familiar dilemma. “You’ve got to take voters from where they are to where you want to go, and the only way to do that is to not dismiss in any way what they know—and what I mean by that is, you can’t go in playing ‘It’s Christmas Time’ when that’s the last holiday they can afford,” Rahm Emanuel, who worked for the Obama and Biden administrations and is a potential contender in the 2028 presidential election, told us. “They’re going to put you on mute.”

In 2010, Barack Obama wrestled with this problem by alighting on a “car in the ditch” metaphor to explain why, after the 2008 financial crisis, the promised recovery still felt slow in coming. Yet even that formulation proved ineffective, Obama’s senior strategist David Axelrod told us. “We sort of abandoned it because what we found was even that was offensive to people, because it felt like we were trying to blame others,” he said. “What we learned very quickly is, you cannot jawbone people into feeling what they do not feel in their own lives, and Biden defied that to his own detriment.”

Trump has shown much more interest in hyperbole than in complicated metaphors, branding his second term in office as a new “Golden Age.” While stumping last Friday for Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, Trump spoke glowingly about his second term. “You have record manufacturing and auto plants being built right now in the United States and in South Carolina,” he said. “We have the greatest economy in our history. Now, some people haven’t seen it yet, but they will.” Axelrod noted that Trump argued at the same rally that his own polling “should be at 100 percent on the economy.” “If you’re the average person out there, you’re seeing that and thinking What planet is he living on?” Axelrod said. “You have to acknowledge that people are struggling and this is a work in progress.”

David Winston, a Republican strategist who works with congressional leadership, told us that key to the midterms is whether voters, when they walk into a grocery store, feel that they can manage at least a little bit better than before Trump returned to office. “So Republicans need to be talking about what actions they took in terms of the economy to at least get things moving in the right direction, and what the outcome has been,” he said. “This is one where it can’t be a laundry list of 35 talking points. This has to be one or two key things.”

Trump’s advisers are hoping to drive home a discrete set of facts about his accomplishments over the past 19 months. The list is likely to include new tax breaks for certain workers and seniors, the stock market’s rise over the past two years, the military’s boat strikes purportedly targeting fentanyl, and his efforts to “seal” the U.S.-Mexico border, to name a few. Rather than distance himself from congressional elections—the preference of some Republican candidates in swing districts—Trump has argued that he can drive turnout in those races by making himself the center of the conversation. Next month, he will host the Republican Party for a two-day “midterm convention” rally in Dallas aimed at nationalizing the November races as a choice between extreme Democrats and Republican accomplishments. Trump has asked his supporters to treat November as though his name is on the ballot. “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” Trump said on Friday in South Carolina. “Just say that I’m on the ballot one more time.”

In other, important ways, Trump is better positioned than either Obama or Biden were at this point in their midterm races. He has a massive cash advantage, thanks to his aggressive fundraising over the first year of his term that collected tens of millions from crypto companies, AI entrepreneurs, and traditional Republican donors. He also enjoys a sharply gerrymandered political map in the House that has created a new cushion of Republican-leaning seats after mid-cycle redistricting. And the Senate majority will be decided by races in Republican-leaning states such as Texas, Alaska, Ohio, and Iowa.

Trump’s advisers have not yet indicated to Republican consultants how much money the president will spend on the midterms, according to people familiar with the matter. But the merits of Trump inserting himself into the election may be less important to some Republicans than the fact that MAGA Inc. is starting to spend. Some in the party have worried for months that Trump might hoard his fundraising for the 2028 presidential-election cycle—or for something else entirely.

MAGA Inc. has begun work on a number of campaigns about specific House and Senate races for the fall. Much of that advertising is expected to feature negative attacks on Democratic candidates, the traditional role of independent super PACs. MAGA Inc. has commissioned polling and research, along with modeling in the targeted House and Senate races. It has also shared information with other independent groups, including the Senate Leadership Fund and the Congressional Leadership Fund, which are affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota and Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana.

In the early spring, Trump’s aides hoped to launch a disciplined sales pitch to voters focused on Trump’s accomplishments, only to have that effort largely derailed by the open-ended Iran conflict. Trump’s approval ratings have eroded further since then. Now is the president’s last chance for a do-over, and his team is projecting confidence that it can get it right. “Anybody that is saying we are headed for a shellacking absolutely can’t just read the numbers,” one of the people familiar with the Oval Office meeting told us. With early voting starting in the first weeks of October, Republicans are once again betting that more Trump is their best way to block Democratic hopes of a wave election.

entries.title: We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built
entries.summary: Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences crave honest voices like hers.
entries.content:
Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences crave honest voices like hers.

Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character.

Parton’s self-construction project began in her childhood. She was born the fourth of 12 kids in a tiny cabin in Pittman Center, Tennessee. Her parents were so poor that they paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. As a girl, she sang songs on her porch into a fake mic fashioned from a tin can and a tobacco stick, envisioning herself at the Grand Ole Opry. Her talent drew attention from local radio and TV personalities, and by age 13, she was singing on the real Opry stage.

The craftiness and self-consciousness that came from growing up impoverished shaped her outlook for life. As she’d sing in her 1971 song “Coat of Many Colors”—her signature (and favorite) hit—her mother used to sew rags into garments that the young Parton would flaunt at school. Mockery from other kids taught her the lesson in self-determination that she’d turn into one of her defining lyrics: “One is only poor only if they choose to be.” As a young woman, she modeled her fashion off a “town tramp”—as she later put it—whom she’d grown up around. Her preacher grandfather whipped her for dressing that way, but to her, women with heels and push-up bras weren’t trashy; they were glamorous and confident.

A fascination with stereotypes—with fulfilling them and subverting them—gave her an edge when she moved to Nashville. In 1966, her first solo hit, “Dumb Blonde” (written by Curly Putman), saw her singing that despite her looks, she “ain’t nobody’s fool.” On the TV variety series The Porter Wagoner Show, she played the aw-shucks second fiddle to the titular star even as she wrote songs that outcompeted Wagoner’s music. Her 1970 hit “Joshua” spun a tale in which the narrator approaches a mean-looking backwoods hermit, someone whom the rest of the town fears, only to realize that he has a heart of gold. It was an example of how her penchant for social criticism and her interest in flipping expectations made her songwriting stand out.

She left Wagoner behind in 1974 to court an audience that transcended country music. Her songs sparkled with fun production touches, clever lyrical twists, and melodies that seemed at once as winding as a lazy river and as smartly constructed as good Levi’s. For 1980’s “9 to 5,” the sound of her fingernail clicks did as much work as the lyrics—and the movie the song accompanied—in celebrating the hustle of women at work. “Jolene,” her enduring ballad of jealousy, built itself around a chorus so plaintive that it seemed surely scraped from a harrowing chapter of Parton’s own life—but she was quick, in interviews, to say that the song’s story was more or less fiction.

As she settled into icon status, she seemed to revel in the franchisability of her image: Dolly Parton was an idea that everyone could benefit from. She founded a theme park in her home state, selling a blend of rustic realness and fun kitsch. She only ever seemed tickled that Whitney Houston’s cover of “I Will Always Love You” eclipsed Parton’s original in eminence. She made childhood literacy the central focus of her philanthropic efforts—another subversion of the “dumb blonde” image (and one that channeled her upbringing by a father who couldn’t read).

In recent years, Parton’s persona has come to take on political significance. She was, as my colleague David Graham has written, the rare public figure who seemed beloved by both red and blue America. She maintained that status through careful circumspection regarding partisan politics. But when it came to questions about sexuality and identity, she took a stand by repeatedly supporting gay, trans, and gender-nonconforming people. After all, she once told RuPaul, she herself was a drag queen.

Many of the most important stories in music this decade owe a lot to Parton. Sabrina Carpenter has brought Dolly-style humor (and hair) back to the charts; Beyoncé enlisted Parton to play emcee on her 2024 album, Cowboy Carter; Ella Langley is blending backwoods scenery with wry, shrugging wisdom that recalls Parton’s catalog. But Parton set an example bigger than music—by showing how to take the scraps you were given and stitch them into something bright and new.
